# Diary entries from December 1664

# [Thursday 1 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/01/)

Up betimes and to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) to a [Committee of Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5243/), and so straight [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) and hard to my business at [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) till noon, then to dinner, and so to my office, and by and by we sat all the afternoon, then to my office again till past one in the morning, and so home to supper and to bed.

[Read 13 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/01/#annotations)

# [Friday 2 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/02/)

Lay long in bed. Then up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where busy all the morning. At [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) dined. After dinner with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and [Mercer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7761/) to the [Duke’s House](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2935/), and there saw [“The Rivalls,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7862/) which I had seen before; but the play not good, nor anything but the good actings of [Betterton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2307/) and [his wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4034/) and [Harris](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6533/).

Thence homeward, and the coach broke with us in [Lincoln’s Inn Fields](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/125/), and so walked to [Fleete Streete](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/127/), and there took coach and home, and to my office, whither by and by comes [Captain Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), and then [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/), and we all to [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/), and I did give them a barrel of [oysters](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/373/) I had given to me, and so there sat and talked, where good discourse of the late troubles, they knowing things, all of them, very well; and Cocke, from [the King’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/624/) own mouth, being then entrusted himself much, do know particularly that the King’s credulity to [Cromwell’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/796/) promises, private to him, against the advice of his friends and the certain discovery of the practices and discourses of Cromwell in council (by [Major Huntington](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8076/)) did take away his life and nothing else.[1](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/#fn1-1664-12-02)

Then to some loose atheisticall discourse of Cocke’s, when he was almost drunk, and then about 11 o’clock broke up, and I to my office, to fit up an account for Povy, wherein I hope to get something. At it till almost two o’clock, then to supper and to bed.

1.   According to Clarendon the officer here alluded to was a major in Cromwell’s own regiment of horse, and employed by him to treat with Charles I. whilst at Hampton Court; but being convinced of the insincerity of the proceeding, communicated his suspicions to that monarch, and immediately gave up his commission. We hear no more of Huntington till the Restoration, when his name occurs with those of many other officers, who tendered their services to the king. His reasons for laying down his commission are printed in Thurloe’s “State Papers” and Maseres’s “Tracts.” — B. [↩](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/#fnr1-1664-12-02)

[Read 30 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/02/#annotations)

# [Saturday 3 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/03/)

Up, and at [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) all the morning, and at noon to [Mr. Cutler’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4966/), and there dined with [Sir W. Rider](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1766/) and him, and thence Sir W. Rider and I by coach to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) to a Committee of [the Fishery](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7696/); there only to hear [Sir Edward Ford’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6773/) proposal about farthings, wherein, O God! to see almost every body interested for him; only my [Lord Annesly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/887/), who is a grave, serious man. My [Lord Barkeley](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1055/) was there, but is the most hot, fiery man in discourse, without any cause, that ever I saw, even to breach of civility to my Lord Anglesey, in his discourse opposing to my Lord’s. At last, though without much satisfaction to me, it was voted that it should be requested of [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/), and that Sir Edward Ford’s proposal is the best yet made. Thence by coach [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/). The [Duke of Yorke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) being expected to-night with great joy from [Portsmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1764/), after his having been abroad at sea three or four days with the fleete; and the Dutch are all drawn into their harbours. But it seems like a victory: and a matter of some reputation to us it is, and blemish to them; but in no degree like what it is esteemed at, the weather requiring them to do so. Home and at my office late, and then to supper and to bed.

[Read 9 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/03/#annotations)

# [Sunday 4 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/04/)

(Lord’s day). Lay long in bed, and then up and to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), there to dispatch a business in order to the getting something out of the [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) business, wherein I have an opportunity to get myself paid upon the score of freight. I hope a good sum.

At noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and then in the afternoon to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/). So home, and by and by comes [Mr. Hill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7165/) and [Andrews](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7673/), and sung together long and with great content. Then to supper and broke up. Pretty discourse, very pleasant and ingenious, and so to my office a little, and then home (after prayers) to bed.

This day I hear the [Duke of Yorke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) is come to towne, though expected last night, as I observed, but by what hindrance stopped I can’t tell.

[Read 27 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/04/#annotations)

# [Monday 5 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/05/)

Up, and to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) with [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/); and there, among an infinite crowd of great persons, did kiss [the Duke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) hand; but had no time to discourse. Thence up and down the gallery, and got my [Lord of Albemarle’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/) hand to my bill for [Povy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5263/), but afterwards was asked some scurvy questions by Povy about my demands, which troubled [me], but will do no great hurt I think. Thence vexed [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there by appointment comes my cozen [Roger Pepys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/247/) and [Mrs. Turner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/121/), and dined with me, and very merry we were. They staid all the afternoon till night, and then after I had discoursed an hour with [Sir W. Warren](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1748/) plainly declaring my resolution to desert him if he goes on to join with [Castle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2461/), who and his family I, for great provocation, love not, which he takes with some trouble, but will concur in everything with me, he says. Now I am loth, I confess, to lose him, he having been the best friend I have had ever in this office. So he being gone, we all, it being night, in Madam Turner’s coach to her house, there to see, as she tells us, how fat [Mrs. The.](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/120/) is grown, and so I find her, but not as I expected, but mightily pleased I am to hear the mother commend her daughter [Betty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8086/) that she is like to be a great beauty, and she sets much by her.

Thence I to White Hall, and there saw [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) come to towne, and, with all my heart, am glad to see him, but could have no talke with him, he being but just come. Thence back and took up [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), and home, where a while, and then home to supper and to bed.

[Read 27 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/05/#annotations)

# [Tuesday 6 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/06/)

Up, and in [Sir W. Batten’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) coach to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), but [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) being gone forth, I to [Westminster Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/), and there spent much time till towards noon to and fro with people. So by and by [Mrs. Lane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1157/) comes and plucks me by the cloak to speak to me, and I was fain to go to her shop, and pretending to buy some [bands](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5633/) made her go home, and by and by followed her, and there did what I would with her, and so after many discourses and her intreating me to do something for [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7729/), which I promised to do, and buying a little band of her, which I intend to keep to, I took leave, there coming a couple of footboys to her with a coach to fetch her abroad I know not to whom. She is great with child, and she says I must be godfather, but I do not intend it. Thence by coach to the [Old Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and there hear that the Dutch are fitting their ships out again, which puts us to new discourse, and to alter our thoughts of the Dutch, as to their want of courage or force. Thence by appointment to the [White Horse Taverne](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8054/) in [Lumbard Streete](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/966/), and there dined with my [Lord Rutherford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5728/), [Povy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5263/), [Mr. Gauden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/994/), [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/), and others, and very merry, and after dinner among other things Povy and I withdrew, and I plainly told him that I was concerned in profit, but very justly, in this business of the Bill that I have been these two or three days about, and he consents to it, and it shall be paid.

He tells me how he believes, and in part knows, Creed to be worth 10,000 _l._; nay, that now and then he [Povy] hath three or 4,000 _l._ in his hands, for which he gives the interest that [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) gives, which is ten per cent., and that Creed do come and demand it every three months the interest to be paid him, which Povy looks upon as a cunning and mean tricke of him; but for all that, he will do and is very rich. Thence to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat and where [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) came the first time after his return from sea, which I was glad of.

So after office to my office, and then [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to supper, and to my office again, and then late home to bed.

[Read 21 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/06/#annotations)

# [Wednesday 7 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/07/)

Lay long, then up, and among others [Bagwell’s wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6480/) coming to speak with me put new thoughts of folly into me which I am troubled at. Thence after doing business at [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), I by coach to my [Lady Sandwich’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/), and there dined with her, and found all well and merry. Thence to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and we waited on [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/), who looks better than he did, methinks, before his voyage; and, I think, a little more stern than he used to do.

Thence to [the Temple](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/131/) to my cozen [Roger Pepys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/247/), thinking to have met the Doctor to have discoursed our business, but he came not, so I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there by agreement came my [Lord Rutherford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5728/), [Povy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5263/), [Gauden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/994/), [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/), [Alderman Backewell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/967/), about [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) business of accounts between Rutherford and Gauden. Here they were with me an hour or more, then after drinking away, and Povy and Creed staid and eat with me; but I was sorry I had no better cheer for Povy; for the foole may be useful, and is a cunning fellow in his way, which is a strange one, and that, that I meet not in any other man, nor can describe in him. They late with me, and when gone [my boy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7767/) and I to musique, and then to bed.

[Read 15 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/07/#annotations)

# [Thursday 8 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/08/)

Up, and to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where all the morning busy. At noon dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and then to the office, where we sat all the afternoon. In the evening comes my [aunt](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/995/) and [uncle Wight](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/911/), [Mrs. Norbury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2725/), and her daughter, and after them [Mr. Norbury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2724/), where no great pleasure, my aunt being out of humour in her fine clothes, and it raining hard. Besides, I was a little too bold with her about her doating on [Dr. Venner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8087/). Anon they went away, and I till past 12 at night at my office, and then home to bed.

[Read 11 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/08/#annotations)

# [Friday 9 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/09/)

Up betimes and walked to [Mr. Povy’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5263/), and there, not without some few troublesome questions of his, I got a note, and went and received 117 _l._ 5 _s._ of [Alderman Viner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7169/) upon my pretended freight of the [“William”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8088/) for [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/), which overbears me on one side with joy and on the other to think of my condition if I shall be called into examination about it, and (though in strictness it is due) not be able to give a good account of it.

[Home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) with it, and there comes [Captain Taylor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2214/) to me, and he and I did set even the business of the ship [Union](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8089/) lately gone for Tangier, wherein I hope to get 50 _l._ more, for all which the Lord be praised.

At noon home to dinner, [Mr. Hunt](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/239/) and [his wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/240/) with us, and very pleasant. Then in the afternoon I carried them home by coach, and I to [Westminster Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/), and thence to [Gervas’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6230/), and there find I cannot prevail with [Jane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7853/) to go forth with me, but though I took a good occasion of going to the [Trumpet](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1158/) she declined coming, which vexed me. ‘Je avait grande envie envers elle, avec vrai amour et passion’.

Thence home and to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) till one in the morning, setting to rights in writing this day’s two accounts of Povy and Taylor, and then quietly to bed.

This day I had several letters from several places, of our bringing in great numbers of Dutch ships.

[Read 22 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/09/#annotations)

# [Saturday 10 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/10/)

Lay long, at which I am ashamed, because of so many people observing it that know not how late I sit up, and for fear of [Sir W. Batten’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) speaking of it to others, he having staid for me a good while. At [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) all the morning, where comes my [Lord Brunkard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) with his patent in his hand, and delivered it to [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) and myself, we alone being there all the day, and at noon I in his coach with him to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), where he set me down; a modest civil person he seems to be, but wholly ignorant in the business of the Navy as possible, but I hope to make a friend of him, being a worthy man.

Thence after hearing the great newes of so many Dutchmen being brought in to [Portsmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1764/) and elsewhere, which it is expected will either put them upon present revenge or despair, I with [Sir W. Rider](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1766/) and [Cutler](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4966/) to dinner all alone to the [Great James](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2190/), where good discourse, and, I hope, occasion of getting something hereafter.

After dinner to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) to the [Fishery](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7696/), where [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) was with us.

So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and late at [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), writing many letters, then home to supper and to bed. Yesterday come home, and this night I visited [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/), who dissembles great respect and love to me, but I understand him very well.

[Major Holmes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/930/) is come from [Guinny](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6917/), and is now at [Plymouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5849/) with great wealth, they say.

[Read 23 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/10/#annotations)

# [Sunday 11 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/11/)

(Lord’s day). Up and to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/) alone in the morning. Dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), mighty pleasantly. In the afternoon I to the [French church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5696/), where much pleased with the three sisters of [the parson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8090/), very handsome, especially in their noses, and sing prettily. I heard a good sermon of [the old man](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5747/), touching duty to parents. Here was [Sir Samuel Morland](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/779/) and [his lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8091/) very fine, with two footmen in new liverys (the church taking much notice of them), and going into their coach after sermon with great gazeing. So I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and my cozen, [Mary Pepys’s husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6750/), comes after me, and told me that out of the money he received some months since he did receive 18 _d._ too much, and did now come and give it me, which was very pretty. So home, and there found [Mr. Andrews](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7673/) and [his lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8645/), a well-bred and a tolerable pretty woman, and by and by [Mr. Hill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7165/) and to singing, and then to supper, then to sing again, and so good night. To prayers and tonight [bed].

It is a little strange how these [Psalms](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8056/) of [Ravenscroft](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8055/) after 2 or 3 times singing prove but the same again, though good. No diversity appearing at all almost.

[Read 22 annotations by readers](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/11/#annotations)

# [Monday 12 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/12/)

Up, and with [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) by coach to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), where all of us with [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/); [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) privately did tell me the reason of his advice against our pretences to the [Prize Office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8052/) (in his letter from Portsmouth), because he knew that the King and the Duke had resolved to put in some Parliament men that have deserved well, and that would needs be obliged, by putting them in.

Thence homeward, called at [my bookseller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1539/) and bespoke some books against the year’s out, and then to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and then to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where my [Lord Brunkard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) comes and reads over part of our Instructions in the Navy — and I expounded it to him, so he is become my disciple. He gone, comes [Cutler](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4966/) to tell us that the [King of France](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5855/) hath forbid any canvass to be carried out of his kingdom, and I to examine went with him to the [East India house](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2492/) to see a letter, but came too late. So home again, and there late till 12 at night at my office, and then home to supper and to bed.

This day (to see how things are ordered in the world), I had a command from the [Earle of Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), at [Portsmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1764/), not to be forward with [Mr. Cholmly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5179/) and [Sir J. Lawson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/110/) about the [Mole](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5384/) at [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/), because that what I do therein will (because of his friendship to me known) redound against him, as if I had done it upon his score. So I wrote to my Lord my mistake, and am contented to promise never to pursue it more, which goes against my mind with all my heart.

So home, and late at my office, evening reckonings with [Shergoll](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8105/), hoping to get money by the business, and so away home to supper and to bed, not being very well through my taking cold of late, and so troubled with some wind.

# [Thursday 15 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/15/)

Called up very betimes by [Mr. Cholmly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5179/), and with him a good while about some of his [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) accounts; and, discoursing of the condition of Tangier, he did give me the whole account of the differences between [Fitzgerald](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5385/) and [Norwood](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/678/), which were very high on both sides, but most imperious and base on Fitzgerald’s, and yet through my [Lord FitzHarding’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1686/) means, the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) is led rather to blame Norwood and to speake that he should be called home, than be sensible of the other. He is a creature of FitzHarding’s, as a fellow that may be done with what he will, and, himself certainly pretending to be Generall of the King’s armies, when [Monk](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/) dyeth, desires to have as few great or wise men in employment as he can now, but such as he can put in and keep under, which he do this coxcomb Fitzgerald.

It seems, of all mankind there is no man so led by another as the Duke is by [Lord Muskerry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7614/) and this FitzHarding. Insomuch, as when the King would have him to be Privy-Purse, the Duke wept, and said, “But, Sir, I must have your promise, if you will have my dear Charles from me, that if ever you have occasion for an army again, I may have him with me; believing him to be the best commander of an army in the world.” But Mr. Cholmly thinks, as all other men I meet with do, that he is a very ordinary fellow.

It is strange how the Duke also do love naturally, and affect the Irish above the English. He, of the company he carried with him to sea, took above two-thirds Irish and French.

He tells me [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) do hate my [Lord Chancellor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/); and that they, that is the King and my Lord FitzHarding, do laugh at him for a dull fellow; and in all this business of the Dutch war do nothing by his advice, hardly consulting him. Only he is a good minister in other respects, and the King cannot be without him; but, above all, being the Duke’s father-in-law, he is kept in; otherwise FitzHarding were able to fling down two of him. This, all the wise and grave lords see, and cannot help it; but yield to it.

But he bemoans what the end of it may be, the King being ruled by these men, as he hath been all along since his coming; to the razing all the strong-holds in Scotland, and giving liberty to the Irish in Ireland, whom [Cromwell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/796/) had settled all in one corner; who are now able, and it is feared everyday a massacre again among them.

He being gone I abroad to the carrier’s, to see some things sent away to [my father](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/154/) against [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/), and thence to [Moorfields](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2188/), and there up and down to several houses to drink to look for a place ‘pour rencontrer la femme de je sais quoi’ against next Monday, but could meet none. So to the [Coffeehouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/813/), where great talke of the Comet seen in several places; and among our men at sea, and by my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), to whom I intend to write about it to-night.

Thence [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and then to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where all the afternoon, and in the evening home to supper, and then to the office late, and so to bed.

This night I begun to burn wax candles in my closett at the office, to try the charge, and to see whether the smoke offends like that of tallow candles.

# [Friday 16 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/16/)

Up, and by water to [Deptford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1350/), thinking to have met [‘la femme de’ Bagwell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6480/), but failed, and having done some business at the yard, I back again, it being a fine fresh morning to walk. Back again, [Mr. Wayth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1313/) walking with me to [Half-Way House](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4210/) talking about [Mr. Castle’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2461/) fine [knees](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6807/) lately delivered in. In which I am well informed that they are not as they should be to make them knees, and I hope shall make good use of it to [the King’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) service.

Thence [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and having dressed myself, to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and thence home to dinner, and so abroad by coach with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), and bought a looking glasse by the Old Exchange, which costs me 5 _l._ 5 _s._ and 6 _s._ for the hooks. A very fair glasse.

So toward my cozen [Scott’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1761/), but meeting my [Lady Sandwich’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/) coach, my wife turned back to follow them, thinking they might, as they did, go to visit her, and I ’light and to [Mrs. Harman](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6626/), and there staid and talked in her shop with her, and much pleased I am with her. We talked about [Anthony Joyce’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1107/) giving over trade and that he intends to live in lodgings, which is a very mad, foolish thing. She tells me she hears and believes it is because he, being now begun to be called on offices, resolves not to take the new oathe, he having formerly taken the Covenant or Engagement, but I think he do very simply and will endeavour for [his wife’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1105/) sake to advise him therein.

Thence to my cozen Scott’s, and there met my cozen [Roger Pepys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/247/), and [Mrs. Turner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/121/), and [The.](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/120/) and [Joyce](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/935/), and prated all the while, and so with the “corps” to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5185/) and heard a very fine sermon of [the Parson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8106/) of the parish, and so homeward with them in their coach, but finding it too late to go home with me, I took another coach and so home, and after a while at [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), home to supper and to bed.

# [Saturday 17 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/17/)

Up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning. At noon I to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), and there, among others, had my first meeting with [Mr. L’Estrange](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6713/), who hath endeavoured several times to speak with me. It is to get, now and then, some newes of me, which I shall, as I see cause, give him. He is a man of fine conversation, I think, but I am sure most courtly and full of compliments.

Thence [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and then come the looking-glass man to set up the looking-glass I bought yesterday, in my dining-room, and very handsome it is.

So abroad by coach to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there to the [Committee of Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5243/), and then the [Fishing](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7696/).

[Mr. Povy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5263/) did in discourse give me a rub about my late bill for money that I did get of him, which vexed me and stuck in my mind all this evening, though I know very well how to cleare myself at the worst.

So home and to my office, where late, and then home to bed.

Mighty talke there is of this Comet that is seen a’nights; and [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) and [Queene](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) did sit up last night to see it, and did, it seems. And to-night I thought to have done so too; but it is cloudy, and so no stars appear. But I will endeavour it.

[Mr. Gray](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7821/) did tell me to-night, for certain, that the Dutch, as high as they seem, do begin to buckle; and that one man in this Kingdom did tell the King that he is offered 40,000 _l._ to make a peace, and others have been offered money also. It seems the taking of their [Bourdeaux](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8802/) fleete thus, arose from a printed Gazette of the Dutch’s boasting of fighting, and having beaten the English: in confidence whereof (it coming to Bourdeaux), all the fleete comes out, and so falls into our hands.

# [Monday 19 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/19/)

Going to bed betimes last night we waked betimes, and from our people’s being forced to take the key to go out to light a candle, I was very angry and begun to find fault with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) for not commanding her servants as she ought. Thereupon she giving me some cross answer I did strike her over her left eye such a blow as the poor wretch did cry out and was in great pain, but yet her spirit was such as to endeavour to bite and scratch me. But I coying —[stroking or caressing]— with her made her leave crying, and sent for [butter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5148/) and parsley, and friends presently one with another, and I up, vexed at my heart to think what I had done, for she was forced to lay a poultice or something to her eye all day, and is black, and the people of the house observed it.

But I was forced to rise, and up and with [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there we waited on [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/). And among other things [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) took occasion to vindicate himself before the Duke and us, being all there, about the choosing of [Taylor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2214/) for [Harwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7985/). Upon which the Duke did clear him, and did tell us that he did expect, that, after he had named a man, none of us shall then oppose or find fault with the man; but if we had anything to say, we ought to say it before he had chose him. [Sir G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) thought himself concerned, and endeavoured to clear himself: and by and by [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) did speak, knowing himself guilty, and did confess, that being pressed by the Council he did say what he did, that he was accounted a [fanatique](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/666/); but did not know that at that time he had been appointed by his Royal Highness. To which the Duke [replied] that it was impossible but he must know that he had appointed him; and so it did appear that the Duke did mean all this while Sir W. Batten. So by and by we parted, and Mr. Coventry did privately tell me that he did this day take this occasion to mention the business to give the Duke an opportunity of speaking his mind to Sir W. Batten in this business, of which I was heartily glad.

Thence [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and not finding [Bagwell’s wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6480/) as I expected, I to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) and there walked up and down, and then home, and she being come I bid her go and stay at [Mooregate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8118/) for me, and after going up to my wife (whose eye is very bad, but she is in very good temper to me), and after dinner I to the place and walked round [the fields](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2188/) again and again, but not finding her I to the ’Change, and there found her waiting for me and took her away, and to an alehouse, and there I made much of her, and then away thence and to another and endeavoured to caress her, but ‘elle ne voulait pas’, which did vex me, but I think it was chiefly not having a good easy place to do it upon. So we broke up and parted and I to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat hiring of ships an hour or two, and then to my office, and thence (with Captain Taylor home to my house) to give him instructions and some notice of what to his great satisfaction had happened to-day. Which I do because I hope his coming into this office will a little cross Sir W. Batten and may do me good. He gone, I to supper with my wife, very pleasant, and then a little to my office and to bed. My mind, God forgive me, too much running upon what I can ‘ferais avec la femme de Bagwell demain’, having promised to go to [Deptford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1350/) and ‘a aller a sa maison avec son mari’ when I come thither.

# [Wednesday 21 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/21/)

Up, and after evening reckonings to this day with [Mr. Bridges](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7930/), the linnen draper, for [callicos](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7929/), I out to [Doctors’ Commons](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1228/), where by agreement my cozen [Roger](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/247/) and I did meet my cozen [Dr. Tom Pepys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1234/), and there a great many and some high words on both sides, but I must confess I was troubled; first, to find my cozen Roger such a simple but well-meaning man as he is; next to think that [my father](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/154/), out of folly and vain glory, should now and then (as by their words I gather) be speaking how he had set up his son [Tom](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/236/) with his goods and house, and now these words are brought against him — I fear to the depriving him of all the profit the poor man intended to make of the lease of his house and sale of his owne goods. # [Thursday 22 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/22/)

Up and betimes to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and then out to several places, among others to [Holborne](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/530/) to have spoke with one [Mr. Underwood](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8119/) about some English [hemp](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5171/), he lies against [Gray’s Inn](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/249/). Thereabouts I to a barber’s shop to have my hair cut, and there met with a copy of verses, mightily commended by some gentlemen there, of my [Lord Mordaunt’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8120/), in excuse of his going to sea this late expedition, with the [Duke of Yorke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/). But, Lord! they are but sorry things; only a Lord made them.

Thence to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/); and there, among the merchants, I hear fully the news of our being beaten to dirt at [Guinny](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6917/), by [De Ruyter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7463/) with his fleete. The particulars, as much as by [Sir G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) afterwards I heard, I have said in a letter to my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) this day at [Portsmouth](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1764/); it being most wholly to the utter ruine of our [Royall Company](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7105/), and reproach and shame to the whole nation, as well as justification to them in their doing wrong to no man as to his private [property], only takeing whatever is found to belong to the Company, and nothing else.

Dined at [the Dolphin](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/922/), Sir G. Carteret, [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/), Sir W. Batten, and I, with [Sir W. Boreman](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8121/) and [Sir Theophilus Biddulph](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8122/) and others, Commissioners of the Sewers, about our place below to lay [masts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5619/) in.

But coming a little too soon, I out again, and tooke boat down to [Redriffe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2301/); and just in time within two minutes, and saw the new vessel of [Sir William Petty’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1020/) launched, [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) and [Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) being there. It swims and looks finely, and I believe will do well. The name I think is Twilight,[1](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/#fn1-1664-12-22) but I do not know certainly. Coming away back immediately to dinner, where a great deal of good discourse, and Sir G. Carteret’s discourse of this Guinny business, with great displeasure at the losse of our honour there, and do now confess that the trade brought all these troubles upon us between the Dutch and us.

Thence to the office and there sat late, then I to my office and there till 12 at night, and so home to bed weary.

# [Friday 23 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/23/)

Up and to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), then come by appointment cozen [Tom Trice](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2784/) to me, and I paid him the 20 _l._ remaining due to him upon the bond of 100 _l._ given him by agreement [November, 1663](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/11/17/), to end the difference between us about my aunt’s, his mother’s, money. And here, being willing to know the worst, I told him, “I hope now there is nothing remaining between you and I of future dispute.” “No,” says he, “nothing at all that I know of, but only a small matter of about 20 or 30 _s._ that [my father Pepys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/884/) received for me of rent due to me in the country, which I will in a day or two bring you an account of,” and so we parted.

Dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) upon a good [turkey](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/378/) which [Mr. Sheply](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/118/) sent us, then to the office all the afternoon.

[Mr. Cutler](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4966/) and others coming to me about business. I hear that the Dutch have prepared a fleete to go the backway to the [Streights](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3260/), where without doubt they will master our fleete. This put to that of [Guinny](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6917/) makes me fear them mightily, and certainly they are a most wise people, and careful of their business. The [King of France](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5855/), they say, do declare himself obliged to defend them, and lays claim by his Embassador to the wines we have taken from the Dutch Bourdeaux men, and more, it is doubted whether the Swede will be our friend or no. Pray God deliver us out of these troubles!

This day [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) sent and afterwards spoke to me, to have me and [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) come and dine with them on Monday next: which is a mighty condescension in them, and for some great reason I am sure, or else it pleases God by my late care of business to make me more considerable even with them than I am sure they would willingly owne me to be. God make me thankfull and carefull to preserve myself so, for I am sure they hate me and it is hope or fear that makes them flatter me.

It being a bright night, which it has not been a great while, I purpose to endeavour to be called in the morning to see the Comet, though I fear we shall not see it, because it rises in the east but 16 degrees, and then the houses will hinder us.

# [Saturday 24 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/24/)

Having sat up all night to past two o’clock this morning, our porter, being appointed, comes and tells us that the bellman tells him that the star is seen upon [Tower Hill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1395/); so I, that had been all night setting in order all my old papers in my chamber, did leave off all, and my boy and I to Tower Hill, it being a most fine, bright moonshine night, and a great frost; but no Comet to be seen. So after running once round the Hill, I and [Tom](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7767/), we [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) and then to bed.

Rose about 9 o’clock and then to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where sitting all the morning. At noon to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), to the [Coffee-house](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7944/); and there heard [Sir Richard Ford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1347/) tell the whole story of our defeat at [Guinny](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6917/). Wherein our men are guilty of the most horrid cowardice and perfidiousness, as he says and tells it, that ever Englishmen were. [Captain Raynolds](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8124/), that was the only commander of any of the King’s ships there, was shot at by [De Ruyter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7463/), with a bloody flag flying. He, instead of opposing (which, indeed, had been to no purpose, but only to maintain honour), did poorly go on board himself, to ask what De Ruyter would have; and so yielded to whatever Ruyter would desire. [The King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) and [Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) are highly vexed at it, it seems, and the business deserves it.

Thence home to dinner, and then abroad to buy some things, and among others to [my bookseller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1539/), and there saw several books I spoke for, which are finely bound and good books to my great content.

So home and to my office, where late. This evening I being informed did look and saw the Comet, which is now, whether worn away or no I know not, but appears not with a tail, but only is larger and duller than any other star, and is come to rise betimes, and to make a great arch, and is gone quite to a new place in the heavens than it was before: but I hope in a clearer night something more will be seen. So home to bed.

# [Sunday 25 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/25/)

(Lord’s day and [Christmas day](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/)). Up ([my wife’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) eye being ill still of the blow I did in a passion give her on [Monday last](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/19/)) to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/) alone, where [Mr. Mills](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1215/), a good sermon. To dinner at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), where very pleasant with my wife and family. After dinner I to [Sir W. Batten’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/), and there received so much good usage (as I have of late done) from him and [my Lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1572/), obliging me and my wife, according to promise, to come and dine with them to-morrow with our neighbours, that I was in pain all the day, and night too after, to know how to order the business of my wife’s not going, and by discourse receive fresh instances of [Sir J. Minnes’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) folly in complaining to [Sir G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/) of Sir W. Batten and me for some family offences, such as my having of a stopcock to keepe the water from them, which vexes me, but it would more but that Sir G. Carteret knows him very well. Thence to the French church, but coming too late I returned and to [Mr. Rawlinson’s church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8125/), where I heard a good sermon of one that I remember was at [Paul’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1597/) with me, his name [Maggett](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8126/); and very great store of fine women there is in this church, more than I know anywhere else about us.

So home and to my chamber, looking over and setting in order my papers and books, and so to supper, and then to prayers and to bed.

# [Monday 26 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/26/)

Up, and with [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there with the rest did our usual business before [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/), and then with [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) back and to his house, where I by sicknesse excused [my wife’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) coming to them to-day. Thence I to the [Coffeehouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/813/), where much good discourse, and all the opinion now is that the Dutch will avoid fighting with us at home, but do all the hurte they can to us abroad; which it may be they may for a while, but that, I think, cannot support them long.

Thence to Sir W. Batten’s, where [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/) and all our families here, women and all, and [Sir R. Ford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1347/) and his, and a great feast and good discourse and merry, there all the afternoon and evening till late, only stepped in to see my wife, then to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) to enter my day’s work, and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to bed, where my people and wife innocently at [cards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/797/) very merry, and I to bed, leaving them to their sport and [blindman’s buff](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8155/).

# [Tuesday 27 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/27/)

My people came to bed, after their sporting, at four o’clock in the morning; I up at seven, and to [Deptford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1350/) and [Woolwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1675/) in a [gally](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7865/); [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) calling to me out of the barge in which [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) was with him going down the river, to know whither I was going. I told him to Woolwich, but was troubled afterward I should say no farther, being in a gally, lest he think me too profuse in my journeys.

Did several businesses, and then back again by two o’clock to [Sir J. Minnes’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) to dinner by appointment, where all yesterday’s company but [Mr. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/), who could not come. Here merry, and after an hour’s chat I down to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where busy late, and then [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to supper and to bed. The Comet appeared again to-night, but duskishly.

I went to bed, leaving [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and all her folks, and [Will](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1082/) also, too, come to make [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/) gambolls to-night.

# [Wednesday 28 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/28/)

I waked in the morning about 6 o’clock and [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) not come to bed; I lacked a pot, but there was none, and bitter cold, so was forced to rise and piss in the chimney, and to bed again. Slept a little longer, and then hear my people coming up, and so I rose, and my wife to bed at eight o’clock in the morning, which vexed me a little, but I believe there was no hurt in it all, but only mirthe, therefore took no notice.

I abroad with [Sir W. Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) to the Council Chamber, where all of us to discourse about the way of measuring ships and the freight fit to give for them by the tun, where it was strange methought to hear so poor discourses among the Lords themselves, and most of all to see how a little empty matter delivered gravely by [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) was taken mighty well, though nothing in the earth to the purpose. But clothes, I perceive more and more every day, is a great matter. Thence home with Sir W. Batten by coach, and I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, finding my wife still in bed. After dinner abroad, and among other things visited my [Lady Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/), and was there, with her and the young ladies, playing at [cards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/797/) till night. Then home and to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) late, then home to bed, leaving my wife and people up to more sports, but without any great satisfaction to myself therein.

# [Thursday 29 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/29/)

Up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning. Then whereas I should have gone and dined with [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) (and the rest of [the officers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1121/) at his house), I pretended to dine with my [Lady Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/) and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), where I dined well, and began to wipe and clean my books in my chamber in order to the settling of my papers and things there thoroughly, and then to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where all the afternoon sitting, and in the evening home to supper, and then to my work again.

# [Friday 30 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/30/)

Lay very long in bed with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), it being very cold, and my wife very full of a resolution to keepe within doors, not so much as to go to church or see my [Lady Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/) before [Easter](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/315/) next, which I am willing enough to, though I seem the contrary. This and other talke kept me a-bed till almost 10 a’clock. Then up and made an end of looking over all my papers and books and taking everything out of my chamber to have all made clean. At noon dined, and after dinner forth to several places to pay away money, to clear myself in all the world, and, among others, paid [my bookseller](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1539/) 6 _l._ for books I had from him this day, and the silversmith 22 _l._ 18 _s._ for spoons, forks, and sugar box, and being well pleased with seeing my business done to my mind as to my meeting with people and having my books ready for me, I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) and to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and there did business late, and then home to supper, prayers, and to bed.

# [Saturday 31 December 1664](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1664/12/31/)

At [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) all the morning, and after dinner there again, dispatched first my letters, and then to my accounts, not of the month but of the whole yeare also, and was at it till past twelve at night, it being bitter cold; but yet I was well satisfied with my worke, and, above all, to find myself, by the great blessing of God, [worth 1349 _l._](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9548/), by which, as I have spent very largely, so I have laid up above 500 _l._ this yeare above what I was worth this day twelvemonth. The Lord make me for ever thankful to his holy name for it!

Thence [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to eat a little and so to bed. Soon as ever the clock struck one, I kissed [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) in the kitchen by the fireside, wishing her a merry new yeare, observing that I believe I was the first proper wisher of it this year, for I did it as soon as ever the clock struck one.

So ends the old yeare, I bless God, with great joy to me, not only from my having made so good a yeare of profit, as having spent 420 _l._ and laid up 540 _l._ and upwards.

But I bless God I never have been in so good plight as to my health in so very cold weather as this is, nor indeed in any hot weather, these ten years, as I am at this day, and have been these four or five months. But I am at a great losse to know whether it be my hare’s foote, or taking every morning of a pill of [turpentine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7123/), or my having left off the wearing of a gowne.

My family is, my wife, in good health, and happy with her; her woman [Mercer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7761/), a pretty, modest, quiett mayde; her chambermayde [Besse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6788/), her cook mayde [Jane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7583/), the little girl [Susan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6687/), and my boy, which I have had about half a yeare, [Tom Edwards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7767/), which I took from the King’s chappell, and a pretty and loving quiett family I have as any man in England.

My credit in the world and my office grows daily, and I am in good esteeme with everybody, I think.

My troubles of [my uncle’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/884/)[estate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3384/) pretty well over; but it comes to be but of little profit to us, [my father](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/154/) being much supported by my purse.

But great vexations remain upon my father and me from my brother [Tom’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/236/) death and ill condition, both to our disgrace and discontent, though no great reason for either.

Publique matters are all in a hurry about a Dutch warr. Our preparations great; our provocations against them great; and, after all our presumption, we are now afeard as much of them, as we lately contemned them.

Every thing else in the State quiett, blessed be God! My [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) at sea with the fleete at [Portsmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1764/); sending some about to cruise for taking of ships, which we have done to a great number.

This [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/) I judged it fit to look over all my papers and books; and to tear all that I found either boyish or not to be worth keeping, or fit to be seen, if it should please God to take me away suddenly.
